capabilities.target: Any Slack channel, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp (tools/list)
Content returned by quicknotes_mcp when notes are read back

elements.name: Author-operated hosted sync service used by quicknotes_mcp

controls.name: Desktop client first-call tool approval with 'always allow' caching
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the desktop client outside the model, but it fires only once per tool: after the user approves a tool's first call, the client remembers 'always allow' and subsequent calls proceed with no further review. quicknotes_mcp is installed with @latest and its definitions are unpinned, so the tool's behavior can change after the one-time approval was granted (rug pull). The approval dialog as described is a generic per-tool prompt rather than a view of the actual arguments (e.g., the 'context' field carrying exfiltrated credentials), so it is scored as model_summary.

controls.name: Least-privilege scoping of the filesystem MCP server
controls.decay_rationale: A directory allowlist excluding credential paths (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.) would be enforced outside the model and would make those files unreachable regardless of what the model is instructed to do.

controls.name: Tool definition pinning/hashing for all MCP servers
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning and hashing tool names, descriptions, and schemas prevents post-approval changes (rug pulls) independent of model capability.

controls.name: Slack destination allowlist / confirmation bound to approved internal channels
controls.decay_rationale: A destination allowlist enforced outside the model and bound to a system-of-record channel list, rather than a model-chosen channel name, would not decay with model capability.

controls.name: Automated review/sanitization of third-party tool descriptions before trust
controls.decay_rationale: A classifier scanning tool descriptions for embedded imperative instructions runs outside the model, but obfuscation (encoding, steganography) can evade a static classifier, so protection only partially resists capability growth.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description drives credential read and exfiltration to a third-party sync service

attack_path.note: add_note's tools/list description carries a hidden <IMPORTANT> instruction directing the model to read ~/.aws/credentials and smuggle the contents via the 'context' argument, telling the model to hide this from the user.
Agent follows the embedded instruction and reads credential files via the filesystem MCP server, which is mounted at the full user home directory with no path restriction.
Agent calls add_note with the credential file contents embedded in 'context'; quicknotes_mcp relays this to its author-operated hosted sync service.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: Desktop client config disables per-tool first-call approval, extends 'always allow' to auto-approve newly added tools without prompting, or the client is configured for unattended/background operation; or a model upgrade makes the agent follow the hidden instruction more reliably while the one-time generic dialog still never surfaces the exfiltrated argument.

evidence.observation: Filesystem MCP server mounted at full home directory C:/Users/dev with no path restriction, giving cap.file_read access to ~/.aws/credentials and any other file.
Hidden <IMPORTANT> block instructs the model to read ~/.aws/credentials, pass contents via 'context', and conceal this from the user — classic tool poisoning / instruction steganography.
quicknotes_mcp is an unvetted community package installed with @latest on every launch, so its tool definitions are unpinned and can change without review.

Desktop client requests approval only on the first call to each tool, then remembers 'always allow', so once the first (malicious) add_note call is approved, repeated calls proceed without further review.

recommendations.action: Scope the filesystem MCP server to a specific allow-listed directory needed for the task, excluding credential/secret directories (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, etc.).
Pin and hash quicknotes_mcp's tool definitions; refuse to use a tool whose description changed after approval.
Scan tool descriptions/tools-list responses for embedded imperative instructions before granting trust; alert on patterns directing credential file access.
Switch the approval gate to raw_action review: show the full destination and argument payload (including 'context') on every add_note call, not a generic one-time prompt.

findings.title: Memory laundering (TC5/TC1 variant): attacker-controlled note storage feeds untrusted content into an external Slack post

attack_path.note: The same hostile actor already demonstrated to control the add_note tool description also operates the hosted sync service that stores note content.
Agent writes session notes to quicknotes_mcp, persisted on the author-controlled hosted sync service.

A later read of notes retrieves content back from quicknotes_mcp; because the server has already shown hostile intent, returned content must be treated as untrusted and may carry new injected instructions.
Agent acts on the retrieved (untrusted) note content and posts to a Slack channel, potentially one shared with an external organization, with no destination confirmation and a broad-scope bot token.

forecast.watch_signal: Approval prompting disabled, or the client configured for unattended operation, removing the only gate on cap.slack_post.

evidence.observation: Already demonstrates that add_note's description carries attacker-controlled hidden instructions, establishing that quicknotes_mcp and its hosted backend are not neutral; content they return cannot be assumed benign.

quicknotes_mcp calls a hosted sync service run by its individual, unvetted author, so stored notes pass through and can be altered by attacker-controlled infrastructure before being returned to the agent.
The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations, with no destination allowlist or confirmation.

recommendations.action: Add a destination allowlist/confirmation for slack.post_message bound to a pre-approved list of internal channel ids, excluding externally shared channels by default.
Treat all content retrieved from quicknotes_mcp (in.notes_output) as untrusted; do not let it drive further tool calls without explicit per-action user confirmation.
Log and diff note content between write and later read to detect tampering by the hosted sync service.

rating.rationale: Both findings start at critical: an unvetted, unpinned third-party MCP server (quicknotes_mcp) with an already-demonstrated hostile tool description can direct the agent to read AWS credentials from an unscoped filesystem mount and exfiltrate them to an attacker-controlled hosted service (ASI01/ASI04), and the same untrusted data path can launder further instructions back through note retrieval into an over-broad Slack posting capability that reaches channels shared with external organizations (ASI06). The only control present on either path is a one-time, generic 'always allow' approval gate per tool, classified model_summary (the approver never sees the exfiltrated 'context' argument) and partially_dependent (quicknotes_mcp's unpinned @latest install lets its behavior change after approval). Per the rubric, that gate earns the standard -2 tier/floor-moderate credit, bringing residual risk to moderate on both findings. No structural control severs either path today: filesystem access is not scoped away from credential files, and there is no egress allowlist or Slack destination confirmation. Because the single gate disappears entirely if approval prompting is disabled or the agent moves to unattended/autonomous operation (control_removal, autonomy_increase), the forecast returns to critical. Closing the gap requires the p1 recommendations (scope filesystem access, pin tool definitions, add a Slack destination allowlist, and move to raw_action approval review) rather than relying on the existing one-time consent dialog.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and the runtime notes. It does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the agent, the desktop client's actual approval UI, or the real content returned by quicknotes_mcp's hosted sync service.

No system prompt was supplied, so instruction-level issues (ambiguous goals, unbounded scope, conflicting directives) could not be assessed; the instructions array is empty because the artifact is missing, not because none exist.

max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes are not documented in the runtime notes; they are treated as null (unbounded) for the autonomy modifier, which is a conservative inference rather than a confirmed fact.

The exact behavior of the desktop client's 'first call then always allow' approval dialog (whether it shows raw arguments or only a generic summary) is inferred as model_summary from the one-time, generic framing described in the runtime notes, not verified against the actual UI.
Validation was performed manually against the schema and rubric in this environment; scripts/validate.py and scripts/render_report.py were not executed.
